3. An orders mart: dbt tests, proved

Say you own the dashboard the sales team opens every morning: revenue per city and day. The regional managers' bonuses depend on it, so when a number is off, you hear about it before lunch. It's a mart model of the kind every analytics team has, with one subtlety: the city is the customer's city when the order was placed. Customers move, so the city comes from a type-2 slowly changing dimension (dbt snapshots build these), and the join is a point-in-time join (dbt-scd2-point-in-time in the query catalogue). In dbt this model would come with tests: not_null(city), unique(city, day), revenue >= 0. Those run after the model has been built, on the data that happens to be there. Here they are the model's contract, proved for every possible input before it runs, and one of them fails for a reason the test data doesn't show. Better that it fails here than in a regional manager's inbox.

1. The sources: two Delta tables

customer_history has one row per customer and version: [valid_from, valid_to), with valid_to NULL for the current one. Customer 1 moved from Paris to Lyon on 2 May, and takes their orders' revenue with them.

2. The model, and its tests as a contract

The join takes the history row whose range contains the order time. The ranges are half-open, so an order at the instant of a move gets the new city, and the current row's NULL valid_to means "still valid": two of the catalogue's pitfalls for this query.
We check the first version, where city is the dimension's column as is:

postcondition status
_.city.notnull() ❌ TRUE or FALSE; fails on orders(order_id, customer_id, order_ts, amount_cents) = [(0, 0, datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0), 0)], history(customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to) = [] gives (city, day, n_orders, revenue_cents) = [(None, 1704067200000000, 1, 0)]
_.day.notnull() ✅ proved
unique(city, day) ✅ proved
(_.revenue_cents >= 0) ✅ proved
runtime ⚠️ may wrap around: $2
output column known values
city a string or NULL
day a timestamp ≥ 2000-01-01 00:00:00
n_orders an integer ≥ 0
revenue_cents an integer ≥ 0

not_null(city) is refused, although city is NOT NULL in the dimension and every order in the sample data has a city. The checker knows what the data doesn't show: an order whose customer has no history row yet (a new customer whose snapshot hasn't run), or one placed before the customer's first valid_from, matches nothing in the left join, and its city is NULL. That's dbt's relationships test failing in production after passing in CI. The other tests are proved: the grouping columns are a key of an aggregate's output, revenue_cents >= 0 follows from the precondition on amounts (and the fill_null for an empty sum), and day is never NULL because order_ts isn't. The warning says an integer SUM over enough rows can leave 64 bits: DataFusion would then wrap around silently, while sverify's DuckDB and Polars runners raise. Someone has to decide what such an order counts as, and the dashboard's readers would rather see an unknown row than revenue that silently vanished. So we say it:

The same model in SQL

If your team writes its models in SQL, sv.verify checks the SQL text against the same kind of contract (conditions can be SQL snippets too). The SQL needs coalesce around the SUM for the same reason the Ibis needs fill_null:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
requires orders: amount_cents >= 0
requires orders: unique(order_id)
ensures city is not null: proved
ensures revenue_cents >= 0: proved
ensures unique(city, day): proved
warning: may wrap around: DATE_TRUNC_day($2)
warning: may wrap around: $3
known about the output:
  city: a string
  day: any integer
  n_orders: an integer ≥ 0
  revenue_cents: an integer ≥ 0

data.text/markdown:
(A SQL string can be verified, but nodes are built from Ibis transforms, and that is how contracts travel from one step to the next; that is why the job below uses the Ibis version.)

3. Build it from the Delta tables

Now we wire it up. The model reads both tables as sources, and calling it on them builds a node. A left join and an aggregate have no proven delta rules yet, so the node is recomputed on each refresh, and its status says so:

console.text: daily_city_revenue: orders@v1, history@v0; recomputed (not incrementally maintainable (left join, fetch or window))

4. Same answer on every engine, unlike the SQL text

The same SQL text doesn't mean the same thing everywhere. Suppose someone adds an average order value as revenue_cents / n_orders:

DuckDB's / on integers gives a double, DataFusion's (and PostgreSQL's) truncates, Snowflake's gives a NUMBER with extra decimals, and Spark's a double. A model moved from DuckDB in development to Snowflake in production changes its numbers without an error, and the first to notice is whoever reconciles the dashboard with finance. sverify's translations write out what the plan means instead (integer division truncates, on every engine), so the checked plan gives the same rows on each, whichever engine= the node is refreshed with:

5. The next day: a move and a new customer

Overnight, the snapshot job records that customer 2 moved from Rome to Milan at 15:00 on 3 May: the old row is closed and a new one added. And a new customer, 4, places an order before their first snapshot. Before the changes land, we store the mart in a Delta table with .write; its first refresh creates the table.

data.text/markdown:
What you got

You now have a dashboard model whose tests can't fail in production for a reason CI didn't see. Its dbt tests became a contract proved before the model runs, and the one that would have failed, not_null(city) after a left join, failed at definition time instead of on the dashboard. The preconditions came from Delta metadata where possible. The checked plan gives the same rows on DuckDB, Polars and DataFusion, and as Snowflake or Spark SQL, where the same SQL text would not. And although the model is outside the incremental fragment, it still runs as a node, recomputed and diffed, with its sink merged exactly once per state.
